title: The Canons of Dort (Condensed)
subtitle: The international Reformed synod's answer (1618–1619) to the five points of the Remonstrance, the document behind what later generations shorthand as the five points of Calvinism.
intro: After Jacob Arminius' death, his followers presented the Dutch churches with a five-article Remonstrance (1610) revising the received Reformed teaching on election, the extent of the atonement, human inability, grace, and perseverance. The National Synod that met at Dordrecht in 1618–1619, with delegates from Britain, Germany, and Switzerland as well as the Netherlands, making it the closest thing to an international council Protestantism has held, answered point by point. The five heads of doctrine below are that answer. The famous TULIP acronym is a much later English mnemonic, not the synod's own outline, and it flattens a document that is more pastoral, more careful, and more generous than its reputation. The condensation below paraphrases each head and its key rejections; it is not the full text.
text:
The following is a condensed summary of the five heads of doctrine. It is a faithful paraphrase, not the full text.

First head: Of divine election. All people sin in Adam and deserve condemnation; God would have done no injustice had he left all to perish. That any are saved is sheer mercy. From eternity, God chose in Christ a definite number of persons, not because he foresaw their faith, but unto faith, out of the common mass, and this election is the fountain of every saving good they receive. The reprobate are passed by and judged for their own sin. The doctrine is to be taught, the synod insists, with reverence and for comfort, not for prying: believers are to find assurance not by climbing into God's secret counsel but by observing in themselves the fruits of election, true faith, godly sorrow, hunger for righteousness.

Second head: Of the death of Christ. Christ's death is of infinite worth and value, abundantly sufficient to expiate the sins of the whole world, the synod says this without embarrassment, and the gospel's promise is to be preached to all people without distinction. Yet it was God's will that the death of his Son should effectually redeem those given to him: the atonement's saving efficacy is for the elect, who are not merely made savable but actually saved by it.

Third and fourth heads: Of human corruption and conversion. Fallen humanity retains reason, conscience, and glimmerings of natural light, but is incapable of any saving good, not sick, but dead in sin, and neither the light of nature nor the law can convert. Conversion is God's work: he not only persuades but penetrates the heart, opens what was closed, softens what was hard, and makes the unwilling willing. And here the synod chooses its words with famous care: this grace does not treat people as blocks and stones, nor take away the will and its properties, but sweetly and powerfully bends it, so that where rebellion ruled, ready obedience begins to reign. Those who come, come freely, because they have been made free.

Fifth head: Of the perseverance of the saints. God does not abandon his work. The converted could not remain standing in their own strength, and they can and do fall into serious sins, the canons name David and Peter, wounding conscience and grieving the Spirit. But God preserves the incorruptible seed; he does not let his own be torn from Christ's hand; and he renews them to repentance. Assurance of perseverance grows from faith in the promises, the Spirit's witness, and a serious pursuit of good works, and this assurance, far from breeding carelessness, is the true root of humility, godliness, and endurance under the cross.

annotations.phrase: not because he foresaw their faith, but unto faith
annotations.note: The exact hinge between the two traditions. The Remonstrants taught election conditioned on foreseen faith; Dort answers that faith is election's result, not its cause. Every Calvinist–Arminian debate since is a footnote to this sentence, and both traditions descend from believers who held their view as biblical conviction, not convenience.

annotations.phrase: abundantly sufficient to expiate the sins of the whole world
annotations.note: Dort's least-known sentence, and a correction to caricature: the synod affirms the infinite sufficiency of the cross and commands indiscriminate gospel preaching. The old formula it echoes, sufficient for all, efficient for the elect, is the canons' actual shape, subtler than the mnemonic's 'limited atonement.'

The synod's description of grace is deliberately anti-mechanical: not coercion of the unwilling but liberation of the enslaved, so that conversion is both entirely God's doing and genuinely the person's own act. Whatever one concludes about the doctrine, the pastoral craftsmanship deserves its due.

A necessary honesty: the five points answer the Remonstrance's five articles; they were never a summary of the Reformed faith, still less of Christianity. This platform files the whole dispute as second-order, Wesley and Whitefield, who divided over exactly this and kept preaching the same gospel, are the working proof that it divides faithful churches, not the faith.
